sections.title: The Race Condition
points: A separate read, check, and write leaves time for another request to change the resource. Both requests can then claim the same item.
Common examples include seats, inventory, bids, and driver assignments. Identify the exact resource that concurrent requests share.
State the rule that must always hold. Enforce its check and update together at the authoritative store.

sections.title: 1) Conditional writes
points: Make a write conditional on current state. For example, decrement inventory only when enough units remain, or claim only an available seat.
Check the affected-row count. Zero changed rows means the claim failed; the database may not raise an error for that result.
A count protects total inventory, not a specific seat. Guard the seat's own row or enforce a unique seat identity.

flows.title: Claim a resource with a conditional write
steps: The service submits a write that includes the required current state, such as available quantity greater than zero.
The database checks that condition and performs the mutation as one atomic operation.
The service checks whether the write changed a row. A zero-row result does not authorize a successful claim.
Related records are inserted only after a successful claim, within the same transaction when required.
After commit, the service confirms success. A conflict requires current-state validation before any bounded retry.

sections.title: 2) Pessimistic locking
points: When application logic must read before deciding, lock the relevant rows first. Validate and update them in one short transaction.
Another writer must wait or skip locked candidates. It cannot independently change the protected rows while the first transaction holds them.
Acquire multiple locks in a consistent order. Handle deadlock or timeout errors with bounded retries of the complete transaction.
Keep payment calls and customer checkout outside the transaction. Store a reservation with an expiry for a longer claim.

flows.title: Update related rows while holding short-lived locks
steps: The service begins a transaction and locks the required rows in a consistent order.
It reads the protected values and checks the business rule.
If the check fails, it rolls back. Otherwise, it writes the related changes.
Commit makes the changes visible under the database's guarantees and releases the locks.
A waiting transaction then proceeds against current state. External payment work stays outside the lock-holding interval.

sections.title: 3) Optimistic concurrency control
points: Optimistic concurrency reads a version with the data. The write succeeds only if that version still matches, then increments it.
A failed version check means another writer changed the record. Reload current state and reconsider the operation before retrying.
Optimistic checks work well when conflicts are rare. Under heavy contention, repeated failed work can cost more than a short lock.
Use a version that changes on every update. A business value that returns to its previous value can hide an intervening change.

sections.title: 4) Isolation levels
points: Read committed prevents dirty reads but does not protect every rule spanning several statements or rows.
Snapshot-style isolation can still allow write skew. Two transactions can update different rows and together violate a shared rule.
Serializable isolation requires a result equivalent to some serial order. The database can abort conflicting transactions; the application must handle retries.
Match isolation and constraints to the actual rule. Another option makes the conflict visible on one shared row that can be guarded.

sections.title: 5) Distributed locks
points: A lease records who holds a resource and when the hold expires. Use it when the claim must outlive a short transaction.
Redis can create a lease atomically with a TTL. A database can conditionally update owner and expiry fields on the resource row.
A stalled holder can resume after its lease expires. Validate current ownership when applying effects; stricter designs may require fencing tokens.
ZooKeeper and etcd provide coordination services with their own failure guarantees. External side effects still need idempotency and recovery.

flows.title: Hold a resource across a longer workflow
steps: The service conditionally records a reservation owner and expiry when the resource is free or its prior lease has expired.
The authoritative store confirms whether this request acquired the claim.
The client completes the longer workflow using that reservation identity.
Before applying an effect, the service checks that the reservation remains current and valid.
It releases only its own current claim. A delayed old holder cannot assume that an expired lease still grants ownership.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Approach
points: Start with a conditional write when one predicate describes the rule. Use a transaction for related writes in the same database.
Choose optimistic checks for rare conflicts. Choose short pessimistic transactions when application decisions and frequent conflicts make retries expensive.
Use serializable isolation or a shared guard row for write skew. Add distributed coordination only when the required boundary demands it.
Separate a short inventory claim from a longer payment workflow. A lease preserves the claim without holding a transaction open.

sections.title: Common Deep Dives
points: Consistent lock order prevents circular waits. Keep lock scope short and retry transactions the database aborts after detecting a deadlock.
A value can change from A to B and back to A. A monotonically increasing version reveals this ABA change.
One hot resource still has a serial capacity limit. A queue can send its requests to one worker at a controlled rate.
More application servers do not increase one row's exclusive write capacity. Split independent inventory or control admission when the product allows it.
Make retries safe when responses disappear after commit. A retry must not repeat a completed charge or create another successful claim.

flows.title: Serialize requests for one hot resource
steps: The server places requests for the same resource in the same Message Queue partition.
One Worker processes that partition in order.
For each request, it checks current database state and commits the permitted change.
It records processing progress after the required output is safe, so a replacement can recover.
Admission must still respect the worker's sustainable rate. The queue smooths bursts without removing the serial capacity limit.

sections.title: Conclusion
points: Describe the invariant, authoritative store, atomic operation, and conflict response together. Include crash recovery and expired ownership.
Choose a primitive that protects the rule during concurrent requests and failures. Keep the protected data in one authoritative store where possible.
